questions.q: In an ER diagram, a relationship set is represented by a:
questions.explanation: A diamond connects the entity sets that take part in the relationship, for example Student - Enrolls - Course.

questions.q: A weak entity set is one that:
options: Does not have enough attributes to form a primary key and depends on an owner entity
questions.explanation: A weak entity has no primary key of its own. It is identified through its owner (strong) entity together with a partial key. Example: a Dependent of an Employee.

questions.q: A weak entity set is represented in an ER diagram by a:
questions.explanation: A double rectangle is used for a weak entity set, and its identifying relationship is drawn as a double diamond.

questions.q: A student can enrol in many courses and each course can have many students. This relationship is:
questions.explanation: Many rows on both sides can be linked to each other, so it is many-to-many. In the relational model it is implemented with a separate junction table.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a one-to-many relationship?
options: One department has many employees, but each employee works in only one department
Each person has exactly one passport and each passport belongs to one person
One student has one roll number
questions.explanation: One department maps to many employees, while each employee maps back to only one department. The second option is one-to-one and the third is many-to-many.

questions.q: Total participation of an entity set in a relationship is shown by a:
questions.explanation: A double line means every entity in the set must take part in the relationship. A single line means partial participation.

questions.q: The network data model represents data as:
options: A strict tree with one parent per child
Records connected by links forming a graph
questions.explanation: In the network model, records are connected by links and form a graph, so a record can take part in many relationships. The hierarchical model allows only a tree.

questions.q: In the network (CODASYL) model, a one-to-many relationship between two record types is implemented using:
questions.explanation: A set links one owner record to many member records. Foreign keys are the relational way of doing the same thing.

questions.q: In the hierarchical data model, every child record has:
options: Parents only at the leaf level
questions.explanation: The hierarchical model is a tree, so each child has one parent and a parent can have many children. Many-to-many relationships are hard to represent in it.

questions.q: The relational model was introduced by:
questions.explanation: E. F. Codd introduced the relational model in 1970. It stores data in relations (tables) and is the basis of SQL.

questions.q: In the relational model, a row of a table is called a:
questions.explanation: Row = tuple, column = attribute, table = relation. Do not mix up the three names.

questions.q: A relation has 5 attributes and 20 tuples. Its degree and cardinality are:
questions.explanation: Degree is the number of attributes (columns) = 5. Cardinality is the number of tuples (rows) = 20.

questions.q: The domain of an attribute is:
options: The number of tuples in a relation
The set of permitted values for that attribute
The primary key of the relation
questions.explanation: A domain is the set of allowed values for an attribute. For example, the domain of Age may be integers from 0 to 120.

questions.q: Which of the following are key features of the object-oriented data model?
questions.explanation: The object-oriented data model stores data as objects with encapsulation (data plus methods), inheritance between classes, and a unique object identity (OID).

questions.q: The entity integrity constraint states that:
options: Every foreign key must be NULL
Every table must have a view
No attribute of the primary key can be NULL
questions.explanation: A primary key identifies each tuple, so it cannot be NULL. A NULL key would mean a tuple that cannot be identified.

questions.q: Referential integrity requires that a foreign key value must:
options: Either match an existing primary key value in the referenced table or be NULL
Always equal the primary key of the same row
Be unique in its own table
questions.explanation: This stops a child row from pointing to a parent row that does not exist, for example an enrolment for a student who is not in the Student table.

questions.q: A super key is:
options: A key that is always a single attribute
A set of one or more attributes that uniquely identifies each tuple
The foreign key of a table
An attribute that can be NULL
questions.explanation: Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple is a super key, even if it has extra attributes. Example: {RollNo, Name} is a super key if RollNo alone is unique.

questions.q: A candidate key is:
questions.explanation: A candidate key is a super key with no unnecessary attribute: if you remove any attribute, it stops being unique.

questions.q: The primary key of a relation is chosen from the:
options: Super keys that have extra attributes
questions.explanation: The designer picks one candidate key to be the primary key. The remaining candidate keys are called alternate keys.

questions.q: A relation has 4 candidate keys. How many primary keys can it have?
questions.explanation: A relation can have many candidate keys but only one primary key. The other three become alternate keys.

questions.q: The CHECK constraint is used to:
options: Restrict the values of a column using a condition, e.g. age >= 18
questions.explanation: CHECK enforces a condition on column values. It is one way of enforcing a domain constraint.

questions.q: Which statement correctly differentiates UNIQUE from PRIMARY KEY?
options: UNIQUE cannot be applied to more than one table
A table can have only one UNIQUE constraint but many primary keys
A UNIQUE column can contain NULL values, while a primary key cannot
UNIQUE columns can never be indexed
questions.explanation: A table has only one primary key (never NULL) but can have many UNIQUE constraints, and UNIQUE columns may hold NULL (exact behaviour varies slightly between DBMS).

questions.q: A child table has a foreign key defined with ON DELETE CASCADE. If a referenced parent row is deleted, then:
options: The matching child rows are also deleted automatically
The foreign key constraint is removed
questions.explanation: CASCADE passes the delete on to the child rows so no orphan rows remain. Without it, the default is usually to reject the delete.

questions.q: Which set lists the basic data manipulation operations?
questions.explanation: The four basic data manipulation operations are insert, delete, modify and retrieve. The first option is DDL and the third is DCL/TCL.

questions.q: Data abstraction in a DBMS means:
options: Compressing the data to save space
Storing all data in a single table
Hiding the complex storage details from users and presenting a simplified view of the data
questions.explanation: Data abstraction hides how data is stored and maintained. It is provided through three levels: physical, logical and view.
